meta.schema_note: One object per day. `wellness` and `activity` are pulled metrics; `score`+`components` per DAY_SCORE.md; `entry` is the coach's read; `prediction`/`pred_half` is the projected half time. reviewed=false means routine-drafted, not yet human-amended.
meta.scoring: probability-change model (DAY_SCORE.md): score=ΔP(1:20), score_committed=ΔP(1:25) — INDEPENDENT trajectories that diverge (neither always higher); 60=neutral; equal-100 ceilings; magnitude discipline; green-recovery floor; decoupling weighted by run type; Pacific tz
meta.timezone: athlete US Pacific (UTC-8/-7); Intervals stores UTC but start_date_local is Pacific; evening runs cross midnight UTC
meta.prob_model: p_120/p_125 = P(hit goal if raced TODAY at current fitness) per DAY_SCORE.md. Both round to ~0% through base phase BY DESIGN — the live signal is pred_half falling toward the goal lines.
meta.model_version: v8: two-invocation; full-resolution streams + Intervals interval structure; raced-today probability; Pacific tz

days.entry: Two runs joined together, and the average hides it. The first twelve kilometres are the run the plan has been asking for: 6:12 to 6:59 per kilometre at 127-145 bpm, genuinely easy, the longest of the block. For context, on July 5 you ran 12 km at 156 HR and called that easy — same athlete, two weeks later, further and fifteen beats lower. That part is the base arriving and it is worth more to this race than anything else you do. Then kilometres 13 to 16 went 4:51, 4:52, 4:37, 4:27 at 160-165 bpm. Split by moving time, the final third covered 6.26 km at 5:15/km and HR 154 against 6:46 and HR 133 for the first — the last 5 km ran 106 s/km quicker than the body of the run. The prescription was 5:50-6:05/km with a heart-rate ceiling of 148. So: a strong session, and 4:27/km at 160 bpm sixteen kilometres deep is real evidence of fitness, but it was a long run with a tempo finish rather than the easy long run it reads as — and embedded quality on long runs isn't due until mid-August. Also worth knowing for reading the numbers: 42 minutes and 39 seconds of the 2h21m elapsed was spent stopped, which is why an average of 141 bpm looks gentler than the running was.

stream_read._method: Segmented on the three recording gaps in the time channel (211 s / 172 s / 200 s) — those gaps ARE the standing recoveries, so they define the reps. Each rep then split at 1000 m to separate the 5K-pace leg from the mile-pace leg. Autolap kilometres were ignored: they straddle rep boundaries and fabricate a mid-set collapse that did not happen.
stream_read.structure: 4 x ~1560 m, each = 1000 m @ 5K pace + ~560 m @ mile pace, ~3 min standing rest
stream_read.cooldown: 1.80 km @ 5:23/km, HR 155 (Z3) — the one loose end; a cooldown should sit in Z1–Z2

components.label: Executed the prescription exactly: every 5K-pace leg landed 3:58-4:02 and every mile-pace leg 3:42 → 3:29. Four reps, four clean gear changes.
Progressive across the whole set — 3:55, 3:53, 3:52, 3:48 — with the closing surge getting faster each rep (20, 20, 24, 29 s/km). Negative-split discipline, not fade.
Held the controlled legs at 4:00, 8-10 s/km SLOWER than 5K pace — resisted the usual pull to over-cook the easy half of a rep
Closing 560 m of the last rep at 3:29/km — comfortably inside mile pace. Genuine speed evidence, which is why 1:20 gains more than 1:25 here.
Recovery depth shrank 62 → 49 → 44 beats across the rests — normal fatigue accumulation through a hard set, not a warning
CTL 27 is still a thin base to be running mile-pace work on; the session is good, the foundation under it is young
Mile-pace sharpening is further from half-marathon specificity than threshold work — right execution, slightly off-target stimulus for the actual limiter
Cooldown at 155 bpm in Z3 — the only sloppy part of the day

days.entry: 4 x 1 mile off three minutes standing, exactly as prescribed, and executed about as well as this session can be. The watch pauses during the recoveries, so the three gaps in the recording — 211, 172 and 200 seconds — mark the reps precisely: four blocks of 366, 363, 362 and 356 seconds. Split each rep at 1000 m and both halves of the assignment show up cleanly. The 5K-pace legs came in at 4:02, 4:00, 4:00, 3:58 — metronomic, and deliberately 8-10 s/km slower than actual 5K pace, which is the discipline this session tests. The mile-pace legs went 3:42, 3:40, 3:36, 3:29: at mile pace, then progressively through it, closing the final 560 m at 3:29/km. Rep averages fell every time (3:55, 3:53, 3:52, 3:48) and the gear change widened every time (20, 20, 24, 29 s/km). That is a negative-split set most runners don't manage. HR climbing 174 to 180 to 183 to 184, with recovery depth shrinking from 62 beats to 44 across the rests, is simply the price of four hard miles — and a 62-beat drop inside three minutes on the first rest is a strong number. Two caveats, neither a criticism of the session: CTL 27 is a young base to be running mile-pace work on, and mile speed is not the limiter here — endurance is. The one loose end is the cooldown at 155 bpm in Z3, which should sit in Z1-Z2. This also firms up the 5K picture: 4 x 1 mile averaging 3:52 off short rest sits with the critical-speed model's 19:07 rather than December's 19:17 being the ceiling.

ATL came off 46.1 to 39.9, form moved from -17.8 — the worst reading of the block — to -12.3, and this morning's resting HR is back to 43, matching the block's floor. That is what a correctly-taken rest day looks like on the numbers. days.entry: Saturday was booked as easy — 50-60 min, HR ceiling 148, tempo gates not open. What actually happened was a full track session: a warmup, then 7x~400m run back-to-back with no real recovery between reps, HR climbing 165 to 180 (95% of max) at a pace (3:57/km) faster than the current threshold estimate and within a few seconds of recent 5K shape. That is a race-effort session by the DAY_SCORE test, run on a day that was supposed to be the cheapest of the week. The cooldown ran brisk rather than easy, so none of the 28 minutes banked toward the aerobic deficit this block exists to close. Recovery was green going in, which limits the immediate risk, but this sets up Sunday's long run on tired legs the day after a maximal effort — exactly the density pattern that has preceded every prior collapse in this athlete's history.
days.note_next: Sunday: the long run is still owed, but it now follows a hard track day. If legs are dead, cut it short rather than force the full 100-110 min — a shorter clean easy run beats a long one run hot on fatigued legs.

stream_read._method: Continuous recording, no watch pauses (moving 6132 s vs elapsed 6133 s). Intervals.icu's own ~1 km auto-laps (20 of them) carry the pace/HR structure; full second-by-second streams were not stored for this file (see gotcha below) — the lap table is complete and internally consistent with the activity summary, so the read below is grounded in real data, not estimated.
stream_read.pacing: 20:13 start (evening). Laps ran 3:12-3:19/km essentially the whole way (avg 5:07/km overall) — this was NOT a back-half fade into hot pace, it was run hot from km 1. Prescribed pace was 5:50-6:05/km; the entire run sat 43-58 s/km faster than that, start to finish.
stream_read.hr_drift: Lap-average HR climbed steadily and almost monotonically: 138 (lap 1) -> 148 -> 150 -> 151 -> 152 -> 154 -> 154 -> 155 -> 154 -> 154 -> 155 -> 157 -> 158 -> 159 -> 159 -> 159 -> 159 -> 159 -> 160 -> 164 (lap 20), peak 168. First-6-lap vs last-6-lap average: 148.8 -> 160.0, a 7.5% rise. Because pace was flat throughout, this is closer to pure cardiac drift from sustained too-hard effort than the 'good decoupling on a clean easy run' signal — the number looks moderate but the context (already-hot pace, not an easy effort) means it should not be read as encouraging.
stream_read.hr_ceiling: Prescribed ceiling 148. The FIRST lap average was already at the ceiling (138 opening, 148 by lap 2); every lap after that ran above it. 65% of the run's time (3916 s) sat in Z3 (153-162), with 333 s in Z4 (162-171). This is a controlled-long-run in name only.
stream_read.milestone: 20.0 km is the longest run of this build and beyond the Sep target of 16-18 km — but it landed 4-5 months ahead of when the plan calls for that distance, and at an effort far harder than 'long', so it reads as an overrun rather than a controlled progression.
stream_read.context: This followed Saturday's unplanned 7x400m session by less than 36 hours — the second hard day in a row, the exact density pattern the plan exists to prevent.

days.entry: This was supposed to be the Jul 18 formula repeated: a controlled long run, HR ceiling 148. Instead it ran 43-58 s/km faster than prescribed for the full 20 km, not just a back-half creep — lap 1 was already at the HR ceiling, and 65% of the run sat in Z3. HR climbed from 139 to 164 across the laps at essentially flat pace, which in this context is cardiac drift from sustained over-effort, not the clean-base signal it would be on a genuinely easy run. It came the day after a maximal-effort track session with no rest between, and it pushed ATL to 50.0 — the worst reading of the entire block, surpassing Friday's previous worst by a wide margin. The 20 km distance is real progress on paper — longest run of the build, ahead of the September target — but it was bought at a cost the plan was built specifically to avoid: two hard days back to back is this athlete's documented collapse pattern, now recurring inside this very build.
days.note_next: Full stand-down is warranted. Whatever the plan said before this weekend, the next session should be decided entirely by tomorrow's recovery numbers, not by the template — expect a red-leaning morning and be ready to take the day fully off.

days.planned: Easy 30 min on flat, familiar ground. HR ceiling 145. No pace target — let the legs set it. Optional 4x20s relaxed strides at the end only if the run has felt clean throughout; skip on any doubt.
days.plan_rationale: This morning's numbers are about as good as this log has ever shown — HRV 115, resting HR at the 41 floor, 8h43m of sleep at score 94. None of that changes today's job. Nine days without a run (nineteen since the 20 km overrun that likely triggered them, twelve since CTL peaked at 30.0 and started falling) means this is a return from a real layoff, not a resumed build — CTL now sits at 23.3, ~7 points under the pre-crash peak. Great recovery numbers on a detrained body are not a green light to chase lost fitness in one session; they mean today's easy run will feel easier than it should, which is exactly the trap. Kept short and genuinely easy, with a hard ceiling rather than a pace target, so the first day back can't quietly become the next intensity spike. General tissue adaptation after any layoff argues the same caution, independent of the tendon's remodeled, load-tolerant status.
days.note_next: If Achilles or calves feel off on waking, or the easy pace wants to creep to hold the ceiling, stop and walk the rest in — day 1 back does not need to be perfect, it needs to be clean. Friday and the rest of the week stay easy-only until several clean sessions are banked; no quality until a full week is absorbed without a flare or a bad night's sleep.
